'''''Encephalartos ferox''''', a member of the family [[Zamiaceae]], is a small cycad with 35 cm wide subterranean trunk. It gets its name from the [[Latin]] word ferocious, likely from the spine-tipped lobes on the leaves of the plant.<ref name="Norstog">Norstog, Knut J., and Trevor J. Nicholls. The Biology of the Cycads. New York : Cornell University Press, 1997.</ref>  It is found naturally on the south-eastern coast of [[Africa]] where it has been used by local people for its starch content.<ref name="jones">Jones, David L. Cycads of the World. Australia: Reed Books, 1993.</ref>  It is considered to be one of the most popular cultivated cycads.<ref name="Norstog"/>

== Naming ==

The species was first described in 1851 when material was collected from [[Mozambique]].<ref>{{cite journal |url=https://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/item/31788#page/312/mode/1up |title=Illustrazione di piante Mozambicesi. Dissertazione II. |first=Giuseppe |last=Bertolini |author-link=Giuseppe Bertoloni |journal=Memorie della Accademia delle Scienze dell'Istituto di Bologna |volume=3 |pages=264–265 |year=1851 |language=Italian}}</ref> After looking at material found in [[Colony of Natal|Natal, South Africa]], it was redescribed as ''E. kosiensis'' <small>Hutchinson</small>. After looking more carefully at the material, the original name was kept, and the redescribed name was no longer used.<ref name="jones"/>

== Habitat ==

''E. ferox'' is found along the southern coast of Mozambique and in northern Natal and can be found very close to the ocean on white beach sand,<ref name="walters">Walters, Terrence, and Roy Osborne. Cycad classification: concepts and recommendations. United Kingdom : CABI Publishing, 2004.</ref>  often growing near other vegetation on the sand dunes.<ref name="Norstog"/>  It is also found in evergreen forests. Its preferred habitat is very humid in the summer and rainfall amounts can range from 1,000 mm to 1,250 mm per year. The climate is more mild in the winter, and it is uncertain whether the species is ever exposed to frost.<ref name="jones"/>

== Leaf, stem and root morphology ==

[[Image:Encephalartos ferox - leaf morphology.jpg|thumb|left|The end of a leaf.]]

The trunk is often subterranean, and can grow up to a meter in length. Its roots contract due to the collapse of transverse sheets of cells in the cortex. It is thought that this contraction can help prevent seedlings from desiccation as they develop.<ref name="Norstog"/>
The leaves are pinnately compound and can grow up to two meters long. They are typically hard-textured, and green.<ref name="Treut">Treutlein, J., Vorster, P., and M. Wink. "Molecular Relationships in ''Encephalartos'' (Zamiaceae, Cycadales) Based on Nucleotide Sequences of Nuclear ITS 1&2, Rbcl, and Genomic ISSR Fingerprinting." Plant Biology 7.1 (2005) : 79-90.</ref>  Young leaves are described as being hairy, and ranging from dark green to coppery brown in color.<ref name="jones"/>  Each leaflet is about 15 cm long and about 3.5 to 5 cm wide. The leaflets can be flat or twisted, and are usually broad with spine-tipped lobes.<ref name="Norstog"/>  They are inserted at about 70° on the rhachis.<ref name="jones"/>

== Reproduction and growth ==

[[Image:Encephalartos ferox - male cone.jpg|thumb|upright|Male cone]]
[[File:20120203 Fairchild EncephalartosFerox Cutler P1180393.jpg|thumb|Female cones]]
[[File:Encephalartos ferox-female-cone-BSI-yercaud-salem-India.JPG|thumb|Female cone, [[Yercaud]], [[Tamil Nadu]].]]
[[File:"Encephalartos_ferox"_Female_Cone.png#/media/File:"Encephalartos_ferox"_Female_Cone.png|thumb|Female cone of ''E. ferox'' subsp. ''ferox'' at Gage Park Tropical Greenhouse in [[Hamilton, Ontario|Hamilton]], [[Ontario]].]]

''E. ferox'' is reported to grow relatively fast compared to members of other cycad genera, but are considered slow-growing when compared to other orders and classes.<ref name="Norstog"/>  
''E. ferox'' reproduces using cones that are of a dark salmon color, as opposed to the greenish coloration typical of other cycads.<ref name="Treut"/>  It shares this coloration with ''[[Encephalartos gratus|E. gratus]]'', although the two species likely evolved this condition independently.<ref name="walters"/>  The cones are sexually dimorphic: the male cone is a 40 to 50 cm long cylinder that is 7 to 10 cm wide with a peduncle that is up to 2 to 3 cm long;  the female cone is 25 to 50 cm long, 20 to 25 cm wide, and sessile. Males can have up to ten cones at one time and females can have up to five cones at one time.<ref name="Norstog"/> The cones also emerge in succession, rather than emerging simultaneously.<ref name="Vor">Vorster, P., Van Der Bank, F. H., Van Der Bank, M. and M. Wink. "Phylogeny of ''Encephalartos'': Some Eastern Cape Species." The Botanical Review 70.2 (2004) : 250-259.</ref>  The shields of the megasporophylls are pyramidal shaped, with flattened facets.<ref name="Norstog"/>  The seeds, which are about 4.5 to 5 cm long and 1.5 to 2 cm wide, are red, narrow, oblong and glossy.<ref name="jones"/>

== Human use and cultivation ==

Cultivation is very popular among ''E. ferox'' since it can be grown fairly easily as long as there is plenty of water, well-drained soil, and moderate temperatures.<ref name="Norstog"/>  It is not very tolerant to frost, and it is best suited in warmer regions.<ref name="jones"/>  They can be propagated from both the seed and from the removal of suckers.<ref name="jones"/> 
Humans have been known to obtain and consume starch that is found in the stem of ''E. ferox''.<ref name="jones"/> It can be used by local people for starch content

== Genetics and evolutionary history ==

''E. ferox'' is not able to hybridize with other species of the genus ''Encephalartos'' very successfully.<ref name="walters"/>  The chromosome number in ''E. ferox'', as well as other species of the genus ''Encephalartos'' for which chromosome number has been found, is 2n = 18.<ref name="walters"/>
It is possible that ''E. ferox'' is most closely related to ''[[Encephalartos arenarius|E. arenarius]]'' due to a similar ecology and similar leaf and cone morphologies.<ref name="Norstog"/>  One study used ''E. ferox'' as an out group in a comparison of eight [[Eastern Cape]] species because it was considered distantly related to those species.<ref name="Vor"/>
